claims.claim: A mathematical model predicts that increasing the half-life of NICD can lead to elevated NICD levels and an increase in the oscillation period.
claims.source: The model predicts that increasing the half-life of the positive regulator, Notch intracellular domain (NICD), can lead to elevated NICD levels and an increase in the oscillation period.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model developed in the study, with numerical solutions shown in Figure 1D-H.

claims.claim: Exposure to XAV939 increases levels of NICD in the chick PSM.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that the level of cNICD protein was increased significantly in the presence of XAV939 (Figure 4D, lanes 5, 6; n = 7/9; Table 1) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool where the resident cNICD had degraded substantially in the presence of cycloheximide.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D and quantified in Table 1, with statistical significance (p = 0.0280).

claims.claim: Exposure to XAV939 prolongs the half-life of NICD in the chick PSM.
claims.source: We observe elevated levels and a prolonged half-life of NICD.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B, where the half-life of cNICD in untreated control embryos is 11.87 (+/− 4.97) minutes.

claims.claim: Reducing NICD production rescues the effects of XAV939 on clock gene oscillations.
claims.source: Reducing NICD production rescues these effects.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that exposure to 1 nM LY411575 together with XAV939 rescues the delay in clock gene oscillations (Figure 8I; n = 6/15).

claims.claim: Somites form with a periodicity of every 90 minutes in the chicken.
claims.source: Mesodermal segments, or somites, 'pinch off' at the rostral limit of the two rods of pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM) that lie on either side of the caudal neural tube, with a distinct, species-specific periodicity; every 90 min in the chicken and every 120 min in the mouse.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, with reference to the broader literature (reviewed in Oates et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Somites form with a periodicity of every 120 minutes in the mouse.
claims.source: Mesodermal segments, or somites, 'pinch off' at the rostral limit of the two rods of pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM) that lie on either side of the caudal neural tube, with a distinct, species-specific periodicity; every 90 min in the chicken and every 120 min in the mouse.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, with reference to the broader literature (reviewed in Oates et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Clock genes belong to the Notch, WNT and FGF signalling pathways.
claims.source: These 'clock' genes belong to the Notch, WNT and FGF signalling pathways and are expressed in a cyclical pattern in the PSM of a wide variety of vertebrate species (Krol et al., 2011; reviewed in Dequéant et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2010; Maroto et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Krol et al., 2011; reviewed in Dequéant et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2010; Maroto et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Oscillatory gene expression in the vertebrate PSM is believed to be established through negative feedback loops of unstable clock gene products.
claims.source: On a single cell level in the vertebrate PSM, oscillatory gene expression is believed to be established through negative feedback loops of unstable clock gene products.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prevailing hypothesis in the field, based on the broader literature context.

claims.claim: The clock period can be altered by genetically modifying genes that encode negative regulators such as Hes7, Her6, Her7, and Nrarp.
claims.source: Subsequent studies have confirmed that the period can be altered by genetically modifying genes that encode negative regulators (e.g., Hes7, Her6, Her7, Nrarp) (Herrgen et al., 2010; Schröter and Oates, 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Takashima et al., 2011; Oates et al., 2012; Harima, et al., 2013; Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Herrgen et al., 2010; Schröter and Oates, 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Takashima et al., 2011; Oates et al., 2012; Harima, et al., 2013; Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013).

claims.claim: Regulation of clock gene mRNA turnover and degradation is gene specific and regulated at the level of the 3′UTR.
claims.source: Moreover, it has been shown that regulation of clock gene mRNA turnover and degradation is gene specific and regulated at the level of the 3′UTR (Hilgers et al., 2005; Nitanda et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hilgers et al., 2005; Nitanda et al., 2014).

claims.claim: There has been relatively little experimental work demonstrating the predicted role of protein stability in regulating the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
claims.source: In contrast, there has been relatively little experimental work demonstrating the predicted role of protein stability in regulating the periodicity of clock gene oscillations (Hirata et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of the field, with only one citation (Hirata et al., 2004) provided as an example.

claims.claim: In zebrafish, Notch plays a key role in the synchronisation of neighbouring oscillators but is not necessary for oscillations themselves.
claims.source: Moreover, in zebrafish there is experimental evidence that Notch plays a key role in the synchronisation of neighbouring oscillators (Delaune et al., 2012) but that it is not necessary for oscillations themselves (Ozbudak and Lewis, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Delaune et al., 2012; Ozbudak and Lewis, 2008).

claims.claim: Notch signalling in mouse and chick is thought to be essential for oscillations.
claims.source: In contrast, Notch signalling in mouse and chick is thought to be essential for oscillations (Ferjentsik et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Ferjentsik et al., 2009).

claims.claim: NICD is unstable.
claims.source: NICD is unstable and, at least in mouse, its production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene (Huppert et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Huppert et al., 2005).

claims.claim: NICD production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene in mouse.
claims.source: NICD is unstable and, at least in mouse, its production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene (Huppert et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Huppert et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Pulsatile Notch1 protein expression is dependent on Notch signalling in the PSM of both chick and mouse.
claims.source: Importantly, pulsatile Notch1 protein expression was recently shown to be dependent on Notch signalling in the PSM of both chick and mouse (Bone et al., 2014); this raises the possibility that, in mouse and chick at least, positive feedback, mediated by Notch and NICD, plays a role in the clock mechanism.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Bone et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In the mathematical model, increasing the NICD half-life increases the period of the oscillation and the levels of both NICD and clock protein.
claims.source: In Figure 1D we show that increasing the NICD half-life increases the period of the oscillation and the levels of both NICD and clock protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: In the mathematical model, increasing the clock protein half-life does not greatly affect the oscillator period but reduces levels of NICD.
claims.source: In Figure 1E we show that increasing the clock protein half-life does not greatly affect the oscillator period but reduces levels of NICD.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: In the mathematical model, the oscillator period and levels of NICD increase with NICD half-life but these effects are not seen upon increasing the clock protein half-life.
claims.source: In Figure 1F,G we show that the oscillator period and levels of NICD increase with NICD half-life but that these effects are not seen upon increasing the clock protein half-life.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1F,G.

claims.claim: In the mathematical model, the increased period arising from increased NICD half-life can be rescued by reducing the NICD production rate.
claims.source: In Figure 1H we show that the increased period, arising as a consequence of increased NICD half-life, can be rescued by reducing the NICD production rate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Treatment with 100 μM XAV939 causes robust and reproducible down regulation of the Wnt target genes cAxin2 and cLef1 in chick PSM explants.
claims.source: Following a titration assay, we determined that 100 μM XAV939 treatment was the lowest concentration that caused robust and reproducible down regulation of the Wnt target genes cAxin2 and cLef1 compared to the corresponding DMSO-treated contralateral explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D; n = 61/68; Bone et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Treatment with 100 μM XAV939 leads to increased levels of phosphorylated β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 in chick PSM explants.
claims.source: Using the same assay, we investigated the effect of the inhibitor on the dynamic expression of cLfng in the PSM. Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression was at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant (Figure 2A, M; n = 57/64) and occasionally this resulted in the treated explant forming one less somite boundary than the control explant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A (n = 8/10; mean fold change = 2.856, p = 0.016).

claims.claim: Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression is at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant in chick PSM.
claims.source: Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression was at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant (Figure 2A, M; n = 57/64) and occasionally this resulted in the treated explant forming one less somite boundary than the control explant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A,M (n = 57/64).

claims.claim: cLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 in chick PSM.
claims.source: In order to ensure that the oscillations were delayed and not halted, a fix and culture assay (see 'Materials and methods') revealed that cLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2B; n = 8/9).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2B (n = 8/9).

claims.claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 100 μM XAV939 treatment in chick PSM.
claims.source: Furthermore, Phospho-histone H3 (pH3) and NucView analyses demonstrated that neither proliferation nor apoptosis, respectively, were significantly affected following drug treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,D; n = 4, p = 0.236; n = 4, p = 0.292).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,D (n = 4, p = 0.236; n = 4, p = 0.292).

claims.claim: Wnt inhibition delays the period of the segmentation clock in the chick PSM.
claims.source: These data clearly demonstrate that Wnt inhibition delays the period of the segmentation clock in the chick PSM.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed cLfng expression following XAV939 treatment.

claims.claim: Exposure to 100 μM XAV939 delays the pace of mLfng oscillations in mouse PSM explants.
claims.source: Using the same half-embryo inhibitor assay in the mouse embryo, we found that exposure to 100 μM XAV939 delayed the pace of mLfng oscillations as compared to control DMSO-treated E10.5 half PSM explants (Figure 2I; n = 19/26).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2I (n = 19/26).

claims.claim: mLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 in mouse PSM.
claims.source: Moreover, a fix and culture assay revealed that mLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2J; n = 12/20).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2J (n = 12/20).

claims.claim: At 25 μM, Cyclopamine abolishes expression of the Shh target gene cGli1 in the chicken half-PSM explant.
claims.source: At 25 μM, Cyclopamine abolished expression of the Shh target gene cGli1 in the chicken half-PSM explant compared to the DMSO control (Figure 3A; n = 5/5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A (n = 5/5).

claims.claim: cLfng expression in the PSM is not delayed by Cyclopamine at either 25 μM or 50 μM.
claims.source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to published data (Resende et al., 2010), cLfng expression in the PSM was not delayed at either 25 μM (Figure 3B,D; n = 6/9) or 50 μM (Figure 3C,D; n = 3/4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B,C,D (n = 6/9 at 25 μM; n = 3/4 at 50 μM).

claims.claim: Shh signalling does not play a direct role in the regulation of the segmentation clock.
claims.source: This assay suggests that Shh signalling does not play a direct role in the regulation of the segmentation clock.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of Cyclopamine on cLfng expression.

claims.claim: NICD stability is known to be regulated by GSK3B in other contexts.
claims.source: Given our results with the Wnt inhibitor and that NICD stability is known, in other contexts, to be regulated by GSK3B (Espinosa et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2009; see also Foltz et al., 2002), we investigated whether the effect upon the period was associated with a change in levels of NICD, as the model predicted.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Espinosa et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2009; see also Foltz et al., 2002).

claims.claim: The anti-cNICD antibody detects a specific band against endogenous cNICD that runs at the same size as recombinant cNICD protein and at the predicted molecular weight of ∼87 kDa.
claims.source: Western Blot revealed a specific band against endogenous cNICD that ran at the same size as recombinant cNICD protein and at the predicted molecular weight of ∼87 kDa in the DMSO control pool which was abolished in the +LY411575 treated pool, thereby validating the specificity of the antibody (Figure 4A, lanes 3, 4; Figure 4D, lanes 1, 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4D.

claims.claim: cNICD exhibits a spatial localisation profile in the chick PSM that is very similar to that described for mNICD in the mouse PSM.
claims.source: We performed immunohistochemistry on sagittal sections of chick PSM tissue to analyse the spatial localisation profile of NICD in this tissue and found it to exhibit a very similar profile to that described for mNICD in the mouse PSM (Huppert et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and comparison to previous work (Huppert et al., 2005).

claims.claim: cNICD is produced in (and cleared from) discrete domains of the PSM in a manner reminiscent of the expression profile of clock genes in different phases of the cycle.
claims.source: Thus cNICD is produced in (and cleared from) discrete domains of the PSM in a manner reminiscent of the expression profile of clock genes in different phases of the cycle (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Exposure to XAV939 elevates the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM.
claims.source: These assays reveal that exposure to XAV939 elevates the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as it delays oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Exposure to Cyclopamine does not affect the levels of cNICD in treated PSM explants.
claims.source: Significantly, exposure to Cyclopamine did not affect the levels of cNICD in treated PSM explants just as it did not affect the pace of cLfng oscillations in this tissue (Figure 4D, lanes 13, 14; n = 2/2; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D, lanes 13, 14 (n = 2/2; Table 1).

claims.claim: Exposure to XAV939 increases the level of mNICD protein in the mouse PSM.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that the level of mNICD protein in the PSM was increased significantly in the presence of XAV939 (Figure 4E, lanes 3, 4; n = 8) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool of half PSM explants, where mNICD levels had dropped substantially in the presence of cycloheximide (Figure 4E, lanes 1, 2; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4E (n = 8) and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: The effect of XAV939 to delay the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and to increase the level of NICD in the PSM is conserved in both chick and mouse.
claims.source: Thus, the effect of XAV939 to delay the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and to increase the level of NICD in the PSM is conserved in both chick and mouse.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects in both chick and mouse.

claims.claim: The stability of NICD in other contexts can be regulated by cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) mediated phosphorylation.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that the stability of NICD in other contexts can be regulated by cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) mediated phosphorylation (Fryer et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Fryer et al., 2004).

claims.claim: Roscovitine is a 2,6,9-substituted purine analogue that competes with ATP for the active binding site on CDKs.
claims.source: Roscovitine is a 2,6,9-substituted purine analogue that competes with ATP for the active binding site on CDKs (MacCallum et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (MacCallum et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Roscovitine treatment at 10 µM clearly delays oscillation of cLfng expression in chick PSM.
claims.source: We found that Roscovitine treatment at 10 µM clearly delayed oscillation of cLfng expression relative to the DMSO control (Figure 2C; n = 59/62)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C (n = 59/62).

claims.claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 10 µM Roscovitine in chick PSM.
claims.source: whilst the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory (Figure 2D; n = 8/10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2D (n = 8/10).

claims.claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 10 µM Roscovitine treatment in chick PSM.
claims.source: Neither proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; n = 5, p = 0.204) nor apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; n = 4, p = 0.886) were significantly affected in the PSM.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,E (n = 5, p = 0.204; n = 4, p = 0.886).

claims.claim: Exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine delays the pace of mLfng oscillations in mouse PSM explants.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine delayed the pace of mLfng oscillations as compared to control DMSO-treated E10.5 mouse half PSM explants (Figure 2K; n = 20/22).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2K (n = 20/22).

claims.claim: mLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 10 μM Roscovitine in mouse PSM.
claims.source: The fix and culture assay revealed that mLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2L; n = 8/10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2L (n = 8/10).

claims.claim: Exposure to 10 μM DRB delays cLfng oscillation phase in chick PSM explants.
claims.source: We found that exposure of chick half-PSM explants to 10 μM DRB delayed cLfng oscillation phase compared to the control explant (Figure 2E; n = 67/73)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E (n = 67/73).

claims.claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 10 μM DRB in chick PSM.
claims.source: and the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory in the PSM at this concentration (Figure 2F; n = 15/18).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2F (n = 15/18).

claims.claim: 10 μM DRB treatment reduces phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II in chick PSM.
claims.source: Western Blotting analysis confirmed that phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II was reduced by 10 μM DRB treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; n = 3/3; mean fold change = 0.709).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (n = 3/3; mean fold change = 0.709).

claims.claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 10 μM DRB treatment in chick PSM.
claims.source: Neither proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; n = 5, p = 0.884) nor apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; n = 3, p = 0.844) were significantly affected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,F (n = 5, p = 0.884; n = 3, p = 0.844).

claims.claim: Exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 reduces phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II in chick PSM.
claims.source: Similarly, exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 reduced phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; n = 2; mean fold change = 0.709)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (n = 2; mean fold change = 0.709).

claims.claim: Exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 delays cLfng oscillation phase in chick PSM explants.
claims.source: delayed cLfng oscillation phase compared to the control half-PSM (Figure 2G; n = 13)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G (n = 13).

claims.claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 1 μM PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
claims.source: and the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory in the PSM at this concentration (Figure 2H; n = 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2H (n = 6).

claims.claim: cHairy2 expression is consistently delayed by treatment with XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
claims.source: Another cycling Notch target, cHairy2, was also consistently delayed compared to the respective DMSO control when treated with either XAV939 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; n = 4/6), Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; n = 6/7), DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; n = 5/6) or PHA-767491 (n = 8/8; Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-D.

claims.claim: A panel of CDK inhibitors robustly delays Notch target clock gene oscillations in the PSM in a manner separable from the cell cycle.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that a panel of CDK inhibitors robustly delays Notch target clock gene oscillations in the PSM in a similar way to that seen following Wnt inhibition and that these effects are separable from the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed clock gene oscillations without significant effects on proliferation or apoptosis.

claims.claim: 100 μM XAV939, 10 μM Roscovitine, and 10 μM DRB robustly down-regulate transcription of cAxin2 in the caudal chicken PSM.
claims.source: We found that 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; n = 31/41) and 10 μM DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; n = 29/42) robustly down-regulated transcription of cAxin2 in the caudal chicken PSM, compared to the DMSO control.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F.

claims.claim: The increased phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 observed with XAV939 is not observed following exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine or 10 μM DRB.
claims.source: However, the increased phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 observed with XAV939, which serves as a readout of Wnt inhibition, was not observed following exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; n = 5/6) or 10 μM DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; n = 4/4)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which Roscovitine and DRB inhibit transcription of cAxin2 is not through the inhibition of canonical Wnt signalling.
claims.source: suggesting that the mechanism by which these CDK inhibitors inhibit transcription of cAxin2 is not through the inhibition of canonical Wnt signalling.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Roscovitine and DRB do not increase phosphorylated β-catenin levels.

claims.claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased significantly in the presence of Roscovitine in chick PSM.
claims.source: Remarkably, and in agreement with model predictions, we observed that the level of cNICD protein was again increased significantly in the presence of Roscovitine (Figure 4D, lanes 7, 8; n = 9/10)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 9/10) and quantified in Table 1 (p = 0.002).

claims.claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased significantly in the presence of DRB in chick PSM.
claims.source: DRB (Figure 4D, lanes 9, 10; n = 6/8)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 6/8) and quantified in Table 1 (p = 0.008).

claims.claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased in the presence of PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
claims.source: and PHA-767491 (Figure 4D, lanes 11, 12; n = 2/2) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool (See Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 2/2) and quantified in Table 1.

claims.claim: Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491 treatments all increase the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as they all delay oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
claims.source: Thus, Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491 treatments all increase the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as they all delay oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing both increased NICD levels and delayed cLfng oscillations.

claims.claim: Increased levels of NICD are associated with an increase to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
claims.source: Hence, taken together the data with the Wnt and CDK inhibitors fulfil the predictions of the model that increased levels of NICD will be associated with an increase to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and model predictions.

claims.claim: Untreated control pairs complete one full oscillation and make an extra somite in 90 min.
claims.source: Untreated control pairs completed one full oscillation and made an extra somite in 90 min whereas exposure to the reagents resulted in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min (n = 8 for each inhibitor and for DMSO; Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J (n = 8).

claims.claim: Exposure to XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491 results in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min in chick PSM.
claims.source: Untreated control pairs completed one full oscillation and made an extra somite in 90 min whereas exposure to the reagents resulted in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min (n = 8 for each inhibitor and for DMSO; Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J (n = 8 for each inhibitor).

claims.claim: A longer clock period will result in the formation of fewer, larger somites in a given time, assuming a constant wave-front speed.
claims.source: A prediction of the clock and wave-front model of somitogenesis is that a longer clock period will result, assuming a constant wave-front speed, in the formation of fewer, larger somites in a given time.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the established clock and wave-front model of somitogenesis.

claims.claim: Fewer somites form in the presence of Roscovitine, DRB, PHA-767491, or XAV939 compared to DMSO controls after 6 hr culture.
claims.source: Hence we analysed somite number in drug-treated explants cultured for an extended period of 6 hr and found that fewer somites formed in the presence of Roscovitine (n = 9, mean number = 2.11), DRB (n = 9, mean number = 1.94), PHA-767491 (n = 10, mean number = 2.5) and XAV939 (n = 7, mean number = 3.14) compared to DMSO controls (n = 15, mean number = 4.25).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by somite counting data after 6 hr culture.

claims.claim: Lfng expression is still dynamic after 6 hr culture in the presence of XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491.
claims.source: Additionally, using the fix and culture assay to confirm that the clock is still operating under treatment conditions, we observed that Lfng expression is still dynamic after the 6 hr culture period (Figure 5D–H; n = 5/5 for each reagent and for DMSO).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 5D-H (n = 5/5 for each reagent).

claims.claim: There is a significant stepwise increase in somite size along the anteroposterior axis in embryos cultured in the presence of XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491 or DRB as compared to DMSO control treated embryos.

results.result: A mathematical model incorporating both positive (NICD) and negative (clock protein) feedback predicts that increasing NICD half-life elevates NICD levels and lengthens oscillation period, while increasing clock protein half-life does not greatly affect period. The model predicts these effects can be rescued by reducing NICD production, and oscillations are only supported within a limited range of NICD and Hes7 half-lives.
results.evaluation: The mathematical model is clearly described with explicit equations and parameters. Numerical solutions in Figure 1D-H demonstrate the predicted behaviors across parameter space. The model provides testable predictions that are subsequently validated experimentally, establishing a strong theoretical framework for the study.

results.result: Treatment with 100 μM XAV939 (a Wnt inhibitor) delays cLfng oscillations in chick PSM by at least one phase, with oscillations remaining dynamic. This effect is specific to the clock mechanism as proliferation and apoptosis are not significantly affected.
results.evaluation: The result is well-supported by in situ hybridization data (n=57/64 showing delay), fix-and-culture assays confirming continued oscillations (n=8/9), and controls showing no significant effects on proliferation (p=0.236) or apoptosis (p=0.292). The experimental design with contralateral controls is rigorous.

results.result: XAV939 treatment delays mLfng oscillations in mouse PSM while maintaining dynamic expression, demonstrating conservation of the Wnt inhibition effect across species.
results.evaluation: The mouse data (n=19/26 showing delay, n=12/20 showing continued dynamics) parallels the chick findings, providing cross-species validation. However, the success rates are somewhat lower than in chick, which could reflect technical challenges or species-specific differences.

results.result: Cyclopamine treatment abolishes Shh target gene expression but does not delay cLfng oscillations or affect cNICD levels, suggesting Shh signaling does not directly regulate the segmentation clock within the 3-hour timeframe tested.
results.evaluation: The data clearly show cGli1 abolishment (n=5/5) but no cLfng delay at 25 μM (n=6/9) or 50 μM (n=3/4), and no change in cNICD levels (n=2/2). This contradicts prior work (Resende et al., 2010) but the authors acknowledge this and provide a plausible explanation based on different culture durations.

results.result: Roscovitine (10 μM), a CDK inhibitor, delays cLfng oscillations in both chick (n=59/62) and mouse (n=20/22) PSM while maintaining oscillatory expression, without significantly affecting proliferation or apoptosis.
results.evaluation: The data are robust with high success rates in both species. Fix-and-culture assays confirm continued oscillations (chick n=8/10, mouse n=8/10). Statistical tests show no significant effects on proliferation (p=0.204) or apoptosis (p=0.886), supporting separation of clock and cell cycle effects.

results.result: DRB (10 μM), a CDK7/9 inhibitor, delays cLfng oscillations (n=67/73) while maintaining oscillatory expression (n=15/18), reduces RNA pol II Ser5 phosphorylation, and does not significantly affect proliferation or apoptosis.
results.evaluation: The result is well-supported with high success rates and appropriate controls. The reduction in RNA pol II Ser5 phosphorylation (n=3/3, fold change=0.709) confirms the drug's mechanism of action. Non-significant effects on proliferation (p=0.884) and apoptosis (p=0.844) support specificity.

results.result: PHA-767491 (1 μM), another CDK7/9 inhibitor, delays cLfng oscillations (n=13) while maintaining oscillatory expression (n=6), reduces RNA pol II Ser5 phosphorylation, and increases cNICD levels (n=2/2).
results.evaluation: The data support the result, though sample sizes are smaller than for other inhibitors (n=13 for delay, n=6 for dynamics, n=2 for NICD). The consistency with DRB and Roscovitine effects strengthens confidence, but the lower n values warrant some caution.

results.result: Multiple CDK inhibitors (XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, PHA-767491) consistently delay cHairy2 expression, demonstrating that CDK inhibition robustly delays Notch target clock gene oscillations in a manner separable from cell cycle effects.
results.evaluation: The consistency across multiple inhibitors and multiple Notch targets (cLfng and cHairy2) strengthens the conclusion. The separation from cell cycle effects is supported by the proliferation and apoptosis data. This represents a key finding linking CDK activity to clock regulation.

results.result: XAV939, Roscovitine, and DRB all down-regulate cAxin2 transcription, but Roscovitine and DRB do not increase β-catenin phosphorylation, suggesting their mechanism of cAxin2 inhibition differs from canonical Wnt pathway inhibition.
results.evaluation: The data clearly show cAxin2 down-regulation by all three inhibitors but differential effects on β-catenin phosphorylation. This is an important mechanistic distinction, though the authors appropriately note they cannot completely rule out alternative Wnt inhibition mechanisms. The logic is sound and the data support the inference.

results.result: XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, and PHA-767491 all significantly increase cNICD protein levels in chick PSM, fulfilling the model prediction that increased NICD levels are associated with increased clock period.
results.evaluation: Western blot data with cycloheximide treatment show significant increases in cNICD for XAV939 (p=0.0280, n=7/9), Roscovitine (p=0.002, n=9/10), and DRB (p=0.008, n=6/8). The consistency across mechanistically distinct inhibitors and agreement with model predictions strongly support this key result.

results.result: XAV939 increases mNICD levels in mouse PSM (n=8), demonstrating conservation of the effect across species and supporting a conserved mechanism linking Wnt inhibition to NICD stabilization and clock delay.
results.evaluation: The mouse data parallel the chick findings, providing important cross-species validation. The sample size (n=8) is adequate and the effect is described as significant in Table 1, though the exact p-value is not provided in the claim text.

results.result: A custom anti-cNICD antibody specifically detects endogenous cNICD at ~87 kDa, and immunohistochemistry reveals cNICD is produced and cleared from discrete PSM domains in a pattern reminiscent of clock gene expression phases.
results.evaluation: Antibody specificity is validated by LY411575 treatment abolishing the band. The spatial localization pattern is similar to published mNICD patterns (Huppert et al., 2005), providing important validation of the antibody and supporting the dynamic nature of NICD in the PSM.

results.result: The increased cNICD levels following inhibitor treatment are not due to increased NICD production, as demonstrated by elevated NICD levels even when new production is blocked with LY411575.
results.evaluation: The experimental design (Figure 4F) directly tests this alternative explanation by blocking new NICD production with LY411575 while treating with inhibitors. The persistence of elevated NICD under these conditions strongly supports the conclusion that the effect is on NICD stability rather than production.

results.result: DRB, Roscovitine, and PHA-767491 significantly increase cNICD half-life from 11.87±4.97 min (control) to 29.59±9.29 min (DRB), 22.01±7.04 min (Roscovitine), and 36.41±8.88 min (PHA-767491), supporting the model prediction that increased NICD half-life results in longer clock period.
results.evaluation: The half-life measurements (n=4-5 per condition) use an appropriate experimental design with cycloheximide to block new synthesis. The increases are substantial (2-3 fold) and statistically significant (asterisks in Figure 6B indicate p<0.05). This is a critical result directly validating the model's central prediction.

results.result: Time-course analysis reveals that untreated control PSM completes one oscillation in 90 min, while XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491 treatment extends the period to approximately 120 min (n=8 for each condition).
results.evaluation: The fix-and-culture time course provides direct measurement of oscillation period. The 90 min control period matches the known chick somite formation period (C6), and the ~33% increase to 120 min with inhibitors is substantial and consistent across all treatments.

results.result: Extended culture (6 hr) with XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491, or DRB results in fewer somites formed, larger somite size, and continued dynamic Lfng expression, consistent with a longer clock period driving altered somitogenesis.
results.evaluation: The data show fewer somites (mean 1.94-3.14 vs 4.25 for DMSO), significant stepwise increases in somite size (p<0.005 for all inhibitors), and continued Lfng dynamics (n=5/5 for each). This provides important phenotypic validation that the clock period changes have biological consequences for somite formation.

results.result: MLN4924 (1 μM), which inhibits SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, delays Lfng oscillations (n=16), increases cNICD levels (n=3), and maintains oscillatory expression. Higher concentrations abolish oscillations, supporting the model prediction that oscillations require balanced NICD levels within a specific range.
results.evaluation: The MLN4924 data provide critical mechanistic validation by targeting NICD degradation through a completely different pathway (ubiquitination). The dose-response (low dose delays, high dose abolishes) elegantly demonstrates the requirement for balanced regulation and validates the model's prediction of a permissive range for oscillations.

results.result: Titration of LY411575 (gamma-secretase inhibitor) shows that 1 nM reduces NICD to control levels when combined with Roscovitine, while 5 nM severely depletes NICD and 0.1 nM has no effect, establishing a dose that can rescue inhibitor-induced NICD elevation.
results.evaluation: The dose-response is well-characterized with Western blot data (Figure 7A-D). The 1 nM dose achieving rescue of NICD levels provides the critical tool for testing causality. This careful titration is essential for the subsequent rescue experiments.

results.result: Co-treatment with 1 nM LY411575 rescues the clock gene oscillation delays caused by Roscovitine (n=15/39), DRB (n=8/20), or XAV939 (n=6/15), while 0.1 nM LY411575 does not rescue, demonstrating that reducing NICD production can reverse the effects of increased NICD half-life.
results.evaluation: The rescue experiments provide critical evidence for causality, directly testing the model's prediction (C91, Figure 1H). The dose-specificity (1 nM rescues, 0.1 nM does not) strengthens the conclusion. However, the rescue rates are modest (15/39, 8/20, 6/15), suggesting the effect may be partial or variable. Despite this, the result strongly supports the causal link between NICD levels and clock period.

results.result: The combined modeling and experimental data support the central thesis that positive regulators (NICD) as well as negative regulators can control clock period, and that tight control of NICD half-life and turnover is key to regulating the pace of clock gene expression.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion integrates the mathematical modeling, pharmacological perturbations, half-life measurements, and rescue experiments. The consistency across multiple independent approaches (different inhibitors, different species, different assays) provides strong support. The data explicitly do not support alternative hypotheses (e.g., effects solely through negative regulators, C105).

results.result: Previous mathematical models based on delayed negative feedback successfully explained many clock observations and predicted that period depends on delays and negative regulator half-lives, but relatively little experimental work has tested the role of protein stability or positive regulators.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize the state of the field based on appropriate citations. They establish the context and rationale for the current study, identifying a gap in experimental validation of protein stability effects and the neglect of positive regulators in prior models.

results.result: Background knowledge establishes that somites form with species-specific periodicity (90 min chick, 120 min mouse), clock genes belong to Notch/WNT/FGF pathways, oscillations involve negative feedback of unstable products, clock period can be altered by modifying negative regulators, and NICD is unstable with pulsatile expression dependent on Notch signaling.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations. They provide essential background for understanding the study's context and novelty. The claims about species-specific periods (C6, C7) are particularly important as they establish the baseline for measuring period changes.

results.result: Prior work has shown that NICD stability can be regulated by GSK3B and CDK-mediated phosphorylation in other contexts, and that NICD is regulated by SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes. Roscovitine and MLN4924 are established inhibitors of CDKs and neddylation, respectively.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately cite relevant prior work establishing the mechanistic basis for the inhibitors used. The citations are appropriate and the knowledge claims are accurate, providing important context for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: MLN4924 elevates phosphorylated β-catenin levels, but the authors propose this is unlikely to mediate the clock effects because phosphorylated β-catenin may remain transcriptionally active in the absence of degradation, as supported by oncogenic APC mutants.
results.evaluation: The data clearly show elevated phosphorylated β-catenin (C81, C129), but the interpretation (C130, C132) is explicitly stated as a proposal/speculation. The supporting evidence from APC mutants (C131) is from a different context (cancer). While the reasoning is plausible, this remains an inference rather than a demonstrated fact. The authors appropriately present this as a proposal rather than a conclusion.

results.result: The authors discuss that increased NICD half-life might alter tissue-scale frequency gradient properties rather than autonomous cellular oscillation frequency, and that positive/negative feedback can enable wide frequency ranges over small amplitude ranges, potentially relevant to the frequency gradient underlying phase waves in somitogenesis.
results.evaluation: These claims (C107, C109) are explicitly presented as possibilities and speculation. While C110 and C111 cite relevant prior work, the application to the current findings remains speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty and note that the central premise (positive regulators can control period) remains valid regardless.

results.result: The authors' findings with XAV939 are discussed in relation to prior work showing LiCl lengthens Hes7 oscillations (possibly via MapK rather than Wnt), CKI-7 delays oscillations, and more specific Wnt activation approaches do not change clock period.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent prior work (Gonzalez et al., 2013; Aulehla et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2009) and appropriately contextualize the current findings. The discussion acknowledges complexities in interpreting Wnt pathway effects and reconciles apparent contradictions in the literature.

results.result: The CDK inhibitors increase NICD half-life and delay clock oscillations at concentrations that do not affect proliferation, with oscillations abolished at higher concentrations that do affect proliferation. This separates clock effects from cell cycle effects and supports the clock-and-wavefront model over cell cycle-based models.
results.evaluation: The dose-response data clearly demonstrate separation of clock and cell cycle effects. The logic connecting this to the clock-and-wavefront model (C121) is sound and supported by appropriate citations. This is an important control addressing a potential confound.

results.result: Recent data showing Notch1 protein is dynamically expressed in a Notch-dependent fashion demonstrate that Notch1/NICD is part of a positive feedback loop.
results.evaluation: The claim accurately cites recent work (Bone et al., 2014) and the inference of positive feedback from Notch-dependent Notch1 expression is logical. This provides important mechanistic context for why NICD should be considered as part of a positive feedback loop in the model.

results.result: Nrarp-null mice display increased NICD levels and decreased somite/vertebral body number, similar to the current findings, though clock period and somite size were not assessed in that study.
results.evaluation: The claim accurately cites prior work (Kim et al., 2011) and appropriately notes what was and was not measured. This provides important independent support for the link between NICD levels and somitogenesis defects.

results.result: Prior work shows that overexpression or complete loss of Notch abolishes oscillations, and together with current data, this indicates a tolerance window for NICD levels that permits oscillations. The current data show that slowing (vs. stopping) oscillations can result from transient/partial NICD stabilization.
results.evaluation: The integration of prior work (C133, appropriately cited) with current findings (dose-response with MLN4924, C85) logically supports the tolerance window concept (C134). The inference about slowing vs. stopping (C135) is well-supported by the data showing maintained oscillations at moderate inhibitor doses.

results.result: While recent work in zebrafish shows tissue shortening rate affects segmentation periodicity, the current data clearly demonstrate that clock pace itself strongly influences somite formation, as evidenced by fewer somites forming when clock oscillations and NICD stability are affected.
results.evaluation: The claim appropriately cites recent zebrafish work (Soroldoni et al., 2014) while maintaining that the current data (C68-C71) clearly show clock pace effects on somite formation. The logic is sound and the data support the conclusion, though the authors appropriately acknowledge the zebrafish findings.
